newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes at fresh eight week highs in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes at fresh eight week highs in U.S.

text.p: After another day of mostly technical buying, the dollar closed at fresh two-month highs versus the mark and yen amid growing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise official U.S. interest rates.
The dollar's push above the key 1.51 mark and 109.45 yen levels came after Federal Reserve Governor Janet Yellen said Tuesday the U.S. economy was in an "inflationary danger zone".

"On a technical basis the dollar looks very solid and there's not any contrary fundamentals that would put a lot of fear into people these days," said Dan O'Connell, vice president at First Chicago NBD Bank.
"The Bundesbank seems to be dollar supportive (as well as) Yellen's comments and the interest rate environment and economic growth picture," O'Connell said.
The dollar derived strength from Monday's remarks by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.
Welteke said the German repo rate could fall if M3 money supply growth slows further, while Tietmeyer suggested G10 central bankers agreed a strong dollar was in their interest.
The dollar closed at 1.5100/10 marks, up from 1.5026/29 at the open and at 109.83/93 yen, up from 109.35/40.
Technical buying spilled over to push the dollar to nearly 110 yen on Tuesday, as against the mark, its highest level since July 16.
Traders said a breach above 110 yen targets a return to 111.20.
Yellen told Reuters she had been surprised by the robust 4.8 percent rate of economic growth so far this year.
Her comments aided widespread market speculation that Fed policy makers are sufficiently worried about rekindled inflation that they will soon raise short-term interest rates.

But Yellen's remarks did not blindside the market, which has been pricing in a Fed credit tighting after several weeks of strong economic data, particulartly a drop in the August unemployment rate to 5.1 percent, from 5.4 percent.

"I guess the expectation is that we are looking at an interest rate hike of a quarter percent," said Tim Summerfield, senior foreign exchange trader at Bank of Boston. "The market is comfortable with it."
The Federal Open Market Committee is expected to agree to raise the fed funds rate to 5.5 percent from its current 5.25 percent, when it meets on September 24.

The dollar broke above the key 1.50 mark barrier on Monday and traders attribute the dollar's continued gains to widespread technical buying, as stop-loss and long-entry trades were executed near 1.5050 and above 1.5110.
"Yellen's remarks may have sparked a little fear but people already new that," said Mary Beth Slack, foreign exchange analyst at consulting firm MCM CurrencyWatch.
"What you are seeing here is largely a technical rally; we broke out two days ago and there has really been no looking back since then," she said.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2348/58 Swiss francs from 1.2273/78 at the open and to Canadian $1.3703/08 from C$1.3689/94.
The pound slipped to $1.5549/56 from $1.5562/72.
The Australian dollar closed at $0.7995/00, slightly up from $0.7993/98.
